ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: food numbers at a glance
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The key food and farming numbers on one page
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: An adult's 1.6 nutrition a day is just under two simple meals.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: These are the numbers you'll reach for most when you plan meals, fields and storage. Each one has its own page, linked below, with the details and what to do about it.

li.heading: Eating
li.text: An adult needs 1.6 nutrition per day and can hold 1.0. Raw food and pemmican give 0.05 per unit; a prepared meal gives 0.9 (lavish 1.0). To get days of food left, divide your total nutrition by 1.6 times the number of mouths.

li.heading: Meals and mood
li.after: Eating without a table costs another -3.

li.heading: Before it rots

table.li: Food | Days before rotting without a freezer

li.after: Spoilage begins above 0 °C and stops at or below 0 °C.

li.heading: Growing
li.text: Plants grow normally at 6 to 42 °C, stop outside 0 to 58 °C, and start dying below -10 °C. They grow only 13 hours a day, so real growth takes about 1.846x the listed grow days. Before sowing late in the season, multiply the crop's listed grow days by 1.846 and check it ripens in time.
li.after: Crops need at least 51% light. A sun lamp draws 2,900 W and covers 24 basins.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: daily nutrition
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: An adult eats 1.6 nutrition a day: about two meals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: If the stock looks like three days of food, plan for two.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A baseline adult needs 1.6 nutrition per day and can hold 1.0 at once, and all your food planning starts from that number. Colonists go looking for food once their food bar falls to 0.25. When it runs out, they become hungry, then malnourished.

li.heading: Meals and raw food
li.text:
Most raw foods and pemmican give 0.05 nutrition per unit. Simple and fine meals give 0.9, lavish meals 1.0. A rough daily ration is therefore 2 meals, or 32 units of raw food or pemmican.
Cooking also stretches your ingredients: a simple meal turns 0.5 raw nutrition into 0.9, so you get back 180% of what goes in. Between that and the mood penalty for eating raw, cook raw food into meals rather than letting people eat it as it is.

li.heading: Keeping track
li.text: Check the Resources panel often and compare the total meals and raw food with the number of mouths. Count prisoners as well; they eat like colonists. In the Needs tab, treat "Hungry" as a warning and "Malnourished" as a failure of the food plan.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: winter stockpile
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Bank about 27 meals per colonist before the fields freeze
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Crops still standing in the field don't count toward the winter stock.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: There's no official "days of food" figure, so you have to do the sums yourself. A colonist eats nearly two meals a day, every day of a 15-day winter, and whatever you store also has to last until you eat it. Plan for rot as well as for mouths.

li.heading: Doing the sums
li.text: At 1.6 nutrition a day and 0.9 per simple meal, a colonist eats about 1.78 meals a day. That makes roughly 27 meals per colonist for a 15-day winter, and about 107 for a full 60-day year.

points.li: Before Septober, divide your food total by your colonist count and compare it with the winter ahead.
For a target, a common rule of thumb is colonists x 1.6 x days without growth, plus about 30% for blight, raids and new mouths.
Add the tame animals that will need hay once grazing stops.

li.after: Keep that buffer even after a good harvest, since toxic fallout or blight can wreck the next one. And don't plan from the quick "10+ tiles per colonist" farming rule: it assumes crops grow all year, so it underfeeds you anywhere with a real winter.

li.heading: Making it last
li.text: Without a freezer, simple meals rot in 4 days, so a stock of cooked meals won't see out a winter. Raw crops keep far longer: potatoes 30 days, rice 40 and corn 60. Pemmican lasts 70, and packaged survival meals barely rot at all. Store raw crops for the long haul and cook as you go, and turn spare meat into pemmican.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: farmland per colonist
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Plan 20 to 25 tiles of food crops per colonist on ordinary soil
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: About 25 tiles of ordinary soil per colonist is a safe starting point.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: How much field each colonist needs depends on soil, crop, grower skill, difficulty and the length of your growing season, which is why the figures you'll hear disagree. Treat every figure here as approximate; lower difficulties need less. Planning for the high end leaves a margin for blight, raids and new colonists.

li.heading: What the sources say
li.text:
A quick rule of thumb says 10+ tiles of food crops per colonist, but that only holds where crops grow all year round.
A more careful figure is 25 tiles of rice, potatoes or corn on ordinary soil to feed one colonist on simple meals. It assumes a Plants 6 grower, prompt harvests and a year-round season on Losing is Fun. On rich soil, 20 tiles of rice or corn does it.
Another reference works it out per crop:

table.li: Crop | Tiles per colonist on soil

li.after: By the same reference, rice needs 15.0 tiles on rich soil and 7.5 in hydroponics.

li.heading: Sizing your own fields
li.text:
Plan about 25 tiles per colonist on soil, then adjust once you see whether your food stock rises or falls. Add 30% to 50% for a short growing season, a low-skill grower or a harsh difficulty. Put food fields on rich soil first; it cuts the area you need.
If your food total falls during the growing season, expand right away. Fields sown in autumn may not ripen before winter.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: meals and mood
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Raw -7, paste -4, fine +5, lavish +12, no table -3
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Eating at a table is worth 3 mood at every meal.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: What people eat, and where they eat it, shows up directly in their mood. A fine meal costs no more raw food than a simple one, so once you have a good cook and both meat and vegetables, the extra mood comes free. Raw food and eating without a table cost mood at every meal.

li.heading: The meals

table.li: Meal | Mood | Nutrition | Raw food it takes
Vegetarian or carnivore fine meal | +5 | 0.9 | 0.75 of one kind (120%)

li.after: Nutrient paste never poisons, but it spoils in 0.75 days. A lavish meal costs as much raw food as it gives.

li.heading: Raw food and the floor
li.text:
Eating raw food gives -7 "ate raw food". Milk, berries and insect jelly are exempt, though they can still poison. Chocolate gives 0.1 nutrition and tastes fine.
Eating without a table costs -3 on top of whatever the meal gives, so give everyone a seat at a table, in a dining room next to the kitchen.

li.heading: What to cook
li.text:
Switch your stove bill to fine meals once a cook reaches Cooking 6 and you have both meat and vegetables. Save lavish meals (Cooking 8) for when mood is in trouble, since they eat into your raw food. Keep nutrient paste for prisoners and food crises, not as the colony's everyday meal.
Without power, a fueled stove burns wood and cooks the same meals as an electric one.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: food poisoning
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Skilled cooks and a clean kitchen prevent most food poisoning
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A cook at Cooking 6 poisons about one meal in 200.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Cooked meals can give food poisoning, and the chance depends on two things you control: the cook's skill and the cleanliness of the room the stove stands in. One bad batch can make several colonists sick on the same day.

li.heading: The cook

table.li: Cooking skill | Chance a meal is poisoned

li.after: Let only your best cook work the stove. A batch bill poisons every meal in the batch together. A bionic stomach halves the chance.

li.heading: The kitchen
li.text:
The dirty-kitchen risk switches off once the stove room's cleanliness is about -2 or better. A butcher table in the kitchen is the usual cause of trouble: it counts as -15 cleanliness on its tile, and butchering spatters blood. In a small kitchen that alone drags cleanliness below -2; in a big room it barely registers. Put the butcher table in its own room, next door to the kitchen.
Floor the kitchen with tile, sterile if you can afford it (each sterile tile adds +0.6 cleanliness), and keep a cleaner on duty. Don't route foot traffic through the kitchen, since colonists track dirt in. If the room stats show the stove room below -2, look for a butcher table or foot traffic first. The same rules apply to a fueled stove or a campfire.

li.heading: Paste and raw food
li.text: Nutrient paste meals never cause food poisoning. Raw food has its own built-in chance, and with Biotech, toxipotatoes double it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: freezer design
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Keep it below 0 °C with spare coolers, thick walls and an airlock
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Food at 0 °C doesn't rot at all. At 1 °C it slowly does.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A freezer stops food rotting entirely, which turns a few days of meals into months of security. Spoilage begins above 0 °C, slows below 10 °C, and stops entirely at or below 0 °C. The hard part is keeping the room below zero through door traffic, heat waves and power cuts, so build it with spare cooling capacity.

li.heading: Building one

points.li: Start at about 6x6, a common size, with room left for the coolers. Bigger rooms need more coolers.
Set the coolers to about -10 °C, so open doors and short power cuts don't push the room above zero. Each cooler draws 200 W.
Vent each cooler's hot side outdoors or into an unroofed gap, never into another room.
Put an airlock, two doors one after the other, between the freezer and the kitchen. It keeps the cold in when people walk through.
In hot climates, double the outer walls; a double-walled freezer holds the cold better.

li.after: With several coolers, staggered targets such as -5 °C and -10 °C let some of them idle on low power.

li.heading: When it fails
li.text: Coolers stop in a solar flare and struggle in a heat wave, so that's when freezers fail. Keep a reserve of pemmican or survival meals for those days.

li.heading: Without power
li.text: An unheated, roofed storeroom freezes on its own in a cold winter. The rest of the year, rely on pemmican: passive coolers can't get a room below 17 °C, so they won't stop rot.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: rot and deterioration
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Heat rots food and open sky wears it down: freezers fix one, roofs the other
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Frozen food left outside still wears away. It needs a roof as well as the cold.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Food can be lost in two separate ways. Spoilage is rot, and it depends on temperature. Deterioration is wear from sitting outside without a roof, and it happens at any temperature.

li.heading: Rot
li.after: Food is safe to eat at any stage before it spoils. Get meat and fish into the freezer the day they come in, since 2 days goes fast, and without a freezer, cook only what you'll eat within 4 days. Every "rotted away" message means your storage is too warm.

li.heading: Wear outdoors
li.text:
Food left under the open sky deteriorates every day: meals by 10, meat and kibble by 6, fish by 3 and pemmican by 2. A roof or a shelf stops it.
The cold doesn't help here. A meal dropped outdoors in freezing weather won't rot, but it will still deteriorate, so keep all food under a roof, even in midwinter.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: growing temperature
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Crops grow best at 6 to 42 °C and start dying below -10 °C
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Healroot survives frosts that kill most food crops.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Temperature decides whether your crops grow at full speed, crawl, or die. Inside the comfortable band they grow normally; outside it growth slows, then stops, and your growers won't sow at all. One hard frost can wipe out a field that was days from harvest.

li.heading: Growth by temperature

table.li: Below -10 °C | Start dying or losing their leaves
Below 0 °C | Stop growing; colonists refuse to sow
0 to 6 °C | Grow at the temperature divided by 6 (half speed at 3 °C)
42 to 58 °C | Grow at (58 minus the temperature) divided by 16
Above 58 °C | Stop growing; colonists refuse to sow

li.after: Heat-resistant plants such as cacti grow up to 75 °C. Select a plant to read its temperature growth multiplier; "Not growing" means it's too hot or too cold. In hot climates, expect crops to stall above 42 °C and plan harvests around the summer peak.

li.heading: Frost
li.text:
Each plant has its own random limit between -18 °C and -10 °C, below which it starts to die. When nights drop toward freezing, harvest anything at 65% growth or more before the frost takes it.
Healroot is cold-resistant, as are nutrifungus and fibercorn with Ideology. Most food crops are not, so in cold climates a heated greenhouse or hydroponics is what keeps food growing through winter.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: growing season
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Plants rest 11 hours a night, so crops take about 1.85x their listed time
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A plant's listed grow days count only the hours it is actually growing.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Plants only grow during the day, so the "grow days" on a plant's info card is not how long you'll actually wait. Your growers also only sow during the zone's growing period, and anything sown too close to its end never ripens. Do the arithmetic before you plant something slow late in the year.

li.heading: Listed days and real days
li.text: Plants rest from hour 19 to hour 5, leaving 13 growing hours a day. Real growth time is therefore about 1.846x the listed grow days: a potato listed at 5.8 days takes about 10.7 days on soil. A crop must reach about 65% growth before it can be harvested.

li.heading: Sowing in time
li.text:
In the northern hemisphere, the growing period usually starts in early Aprimay and ends in mid or late Septober. Select a growing zone to see its local growing period before you choose what to plant.
Late in the season, sow fast rice instead of slow corn, and switch off sowing on zones near the end of the season so your growers' work isn't wasted.

li.heading: Crops left standing
li.text: A plant lives for its grow days times a lifespan factor (usually 5, up to 8), so an unharvested crop eventually dies. Keep enough growers on duty that ripe crops are cut before they die of old age.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: soil fertility
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Rich soil 140%, soil 100%, gravel 70%, hydroponics 280%
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Rich soil grows rice and corn 40% faster than ordinary soil.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Fertility is how fast plants grow on a tile. It changes growth speed, not how much each plant yields, so better soil means more harvests a year. How much a crop gains also depends on its fertility sensitivity.

li.heading: Fertility by ground
li.after: Most crops need at least 50% fertility (trees 30%), so nothing farms on sand.

li.heading: How much a crop gains
li.text: A crop's growth from soil is (fertility - 100%) x its fertility sensitivity + 100%. On gravel, potatoes grow at 88% speed and rice at 70%. Put soil-sensitive crops such as rice and corn on the best ground, and potatoes on gravel.

li.heading: Laying out fields
li.text: Hover over tiles to read terrain and fertility before you lay out fields. Zone your rich soil patches first, and never build over them. Growing zones can't go on sand, mud, ice, bare stone, water or built floors, so don't lay floors where you plan to farm, and remove any that are already there before you zone the field.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: matching crops to soil
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Potatoes barely slow down on poor soil; rice and corn need good ground
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: On gravel and stony soil, potatoes lose the least speed of the staple crops.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Each crop has a fertility sensitivity that says how much it cares about the ground. At 1.0, a crop grows exactly as fast as the soil allows; a low number means it barely notices. On 70% gravel, potatoes grow at 88% speed while rice and corn grow at 70%, so matching crops to soil gets more food from the same fields.

table.li: Toxipotato (Biotech) | 0, so it ignores soil entirely
Rice, corn, cotton, healroot, smokeleaf, strawberry, devilstrand | 1.0

li.heading: Where to plant what

points.li: Stony soil and gravel: potatoes.
Rich soil: rice, corn, cotton and healroot.
Hydroponics basins: rice.

li.after: Before you commit a new crop to poor ground, read "Fertility sensitivity" on its info card.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: rice
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The fastest food crop: first harvest, last harvest, and hydroponics
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Rice ripens in about 5.5 days, faster than any other food crop.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Rice ripens faster than any other food crop, which makes it the usual choice for a new colony's first harvest and for a last one before winter. Each harvest is small, so a blight or fire costs you less, but your growers will be busy: rice needs more harvesting work than corn for the same amount of food.

li.heading: Growth and yield
li.text: Rice takes 3 listed grow days, about 5.5 real days, and yields 6 rice per plant. With a fertility sensitivity of 1.0, it gets the full benefit of good ground. Raw rice rots in 40 days.

table.li: Ground | Harvest per tile per day

li.heading: When to plant it
li.text: Plant rice first in a new colony, before anything else edible, and sow it again late in the season when slower crops wouldn't ripen in time. It's also the best crop for hydroponics, so make it your basin staple. Keep it on soil or rich soil; on gravel, potatoes do better.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: potatoes
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The crop for poor soil: barely slowed by gravel
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Potatoes are the staple crop for rocky maps.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Potatoes care little about soil, so they lose only a bit of speed on stony soil or gravel where rice and corn struggle. That makes them the natural staple on rocky maps. In hydroponics, though, they waste most of the basin's bonus.

li.text:
Potatoes take 5.8 listed grow days, about 10.7 real days, and yield 11 potatoes per plant. Their fertility sensitivity is only 0.4, so they harvest 0.90 per tile per day on gravel, hardly less than the 1.03 they manage on soil. Rich soil lifts them only to 1.19, which is why it's better spent on rice or corn while potatoes go on gravel and stony soil.
In hydroponics they reach 1.77, only about 58% of what rice does, so keep potatoes for outdoor fields and use the basins for rice. Raw potatoes rot in 30 days; freeze or cook a big harvest before then.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: corn
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Little work per meal and keeps 60 days, but slow and fragile
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Corn needs about three weeks to ripen, so it has to go in early.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Corn takes a long time to grow, but each plant gives a big harvest, so your growers spend less time per meal. It also keeps for 60 days raw, the longest of the staple crops. On the other hand, a blight or fire destroys a lot of food in one go, and corn sown late in the season never ripens.

li.heading: How it grows
li.text: Corn takes 11.3 listed grow days, about 20.9 real days, and yields 22 corn per plant. Its fertility sensitivity is 1.0, so it suffers on poor ground: it harvests 0.74 per tile per day on gravel, 1.05 on soil and 1.48 on rich soil. It can't be grown in hydroponics.

points.li: Sow corn early in the growing season. Late in the year, plant rice instead.
Choose it when you have plenty of soil but few growers.
Give it rich soil, not gravel.
Split it into several fields with gaps, so one blight or fire can't take the lot.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: preserved food
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Pemmican lasts 70 days and survival meals barely rot at all
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Pemmican costs more raw food than a fine meal, but it needs no freezer.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: When you have no freezer, a long caravan ahead, or a winter you don't trust, you want food that keeps. Pemmican and packaged survival meals last far longer than ordinary meals. They use more raw food than fine meals, so treat them as insurance, not a daily diet.

li.heading: What long life costs
li.text: Pemmican is made 16 at a time from 0.25 meat plus 0.25 vegetable nutrition, and gives 0.05 nutrition per unit. A packaged survival meal gives 0.9 nutrition from 0.3 meat plus 0.3 vegetable nutrition, and tastes "Simple".

table.li: Food | Food back | How long it keeps
Simple or fine meal | 180% | Rots in 4 days without a freezer
Pemmican | about 160% | Rots after 70 days; deteriorates 2 a day outdoors
Packaged survival meal | 150% | Effectively never rots; deteriorates only 0.25 a day

li.after: Compared with an ordinary meal, pemmican and survival meals cost you some food for their long life.

li.heading: Kibble
li.text: Kibble is for animals only. It's made 50 units at a time, each worth 0.05 nutrition, from 1 meat or animal product plus 1 vegetable or hay nutrition (125%).

li.heading: When to use them

points.li: Without power, turn spare meat and vegetables into pemmican before they rot.
Pack pemmican or survival meals for any caravan that will be out more than a few days.
Keep a stash of non-perishable food for solar flares, heat waves and freezer failures.

li.after: Store it under a roof; even long-lasting food wears away outdoors.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: blight and field safety
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Leave 4-tile gaps between fields and clear brush around them
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Blight spreads to any crop, not just plants of the same kind.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Besides winter, your fields face three big threats: blight, fire and toxic fallout. Gaps between fields and cleared ground around them decide whether you lose a corner or the whole harvest.

li.heading: Blight
li.text: Blight can spread to crops of any kind within a 4-tile radius. Leave 4-tile gaps between fields, or split big fields into separate blocks, and cut blighted plants the moment the blight letter arrives. Rice's small, frequent harvests make it the most blight-tolerant crop.

li.heading: Fire
li.text: Raiders set growing zones on fire. Clear wild plants and flammable items within at least 2 tiles of your fields, and consider firefoam poppers.

li.heading: Fallout and weather
li.text: Toxic fallout and bad temperatures kill crops; drought does not. Build roofed walkways between the kitchen and the fields for winter and toxic fallout.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: hydroponics basin
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: 280% fertility indoors, as long as the power holds
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A basin draws 70 W day and night, on top of the sun lamp.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A hydroponics basin is an indoor planter that grows crops nearly three times as fast as ordinary soil. It lets mountain bases and frozen maps farm all year. Its weak point is power: when the electricity goes, the plants die within hours.

li.heading: Building one
li.text:
Hydroponics research costs 700 points, or 1,400 for tribal starts. A basin then costs 100 steel and 1 component and needs Construction 4. It acts as 280% fertility soil, holds 4 plants and draws 70 W day and night. It has a cleanliness of -3 and can't be uninstalled, so place it where you mean to keep it.
Put basins in a roofed room with a sun lamp and a heater for winter. Grow rice or strawberries in them, not potatoes; corn, devilstrand and haygrass can't be grown in a basin at all. On a tribal start, use a partly unroofed greenhouse until you can afford the research.

li.heading: When the power goes
li.text: Without power, the plants rot and mostly die within about 8 hours, so a long solar flare can wipe them out. Keep batteries or a backup generator; basins can't wait out a long blackout.

li.heading: With Biotech and Odyssey
li.text: With Biotech, basins don't protect crops from pollution, except psychoid and toxipotato. With Odyssey, basins ignore drought and are the only way to farm on a gravship.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: basins per colonist
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: About 2 basins of rice under a sun lamp feed one colonist
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: One sun lamp over 24 basins of rice feeds about twelve colonists.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: If hydroponics feeds your colony, you need to know how many basins one person eats. Rice is the most productive basin crop, and one and a half to two basins of it keep a colonist in simple meals. Build slightly more than the bare minimum, so one lost harvest doesn't leave anyone hungry.

li.heading: The arithmetic
li.text:
A basin of rice gives 24 rice about every 1.98 days: about 12.1 rice, or 0.61 nutrition, a day. Cooked into simple meals, one colonist's 1.6 nutrition a day needs about 1.5 basins of rice. A more cautious reference figure is 7.5 plant tiles per colonist, about 1.9 basins.
So plan 2 basins of rice per colonist if hydroponics is your main food source.

table.li: Crop | Food per basin per day

li.heading: As the colony grows
li.text: Add basins for prisoners and new recruits before they arrive, not after. For a few days after building, watch the food total in the Resources panel; if it still falls, add basins.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: sun lamps and light
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Crops need 51% light; a sun lamp gives 100% over up to 24 basins
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Standing lamps give 50% light, and crops need 51%.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Crops need bright light, and ordinary lamps aren't bright enough. Most plants need at least 51% light to grow, while standing lamps give at most 50% and don't stack. Only decorative plants, and with Ideology tinctoria and fibercorn, manage at 50%. Indoors, a sun lamp is the only way to grow food.

li.heading: The sun lamp
li.text: A sun lamp gives 100% light in its radius and draws 2,900 W for about 13 hours a day, which makes it one of the hungriest buildings on your grid. One lamp covers up to 24 basins, so arrange basins in a ring around it to get the most from its power. Make sure your grid can carry the lamp before you switch it on.

li.heading: Letting the sun in
li.text: A greenhouse can leave up to a quarter of its tiles unroofed (at most 300) to use daylight instead of a sun lamp and to grow trees, at a higher heating cost. Without electricity, that's how you farm indoors: leave up to a quarter of the roof open and heat the greenhouse through the winter.

li.heading: Mushrooms
li.text: Glowstool, agarilux, and nutrifungus with Ideology need no light at all, and they die under any light that isn't meant for mushrooms. Grow them in a dark room of their own.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: feeding animals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Grazing stops in winter; stock hay or kibble before it does
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Snow and leafless winter plants leave grazing animals nothing to eat.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Grazing animals feed themselves from mature plants most of the year, but in winter plants go leafless and snow can bury them. Without stored hay or kibble, your animals go hungry, then malnourished. Malnutrition means slower growth, miscarriages, health problems, and finally starvation.

li.heading: Grazing
li.text:
Herbivores graze mature plants, usually from about 65% growth, in pens, near hitching posts or in their allowed area. In winter, leafless plants can't be eaten and deep snow can block grazing.
Hungry animals, wild or tame, also help themselves to standing crops. Fence your crops, or restrict animals to areas away from the fields.

li.heading: Hay and kibble
li.text:
Before winter, stockpile hay for herbivores and kibble for carnivores. Both give 0.05 nutrition per unit; kibble is made from meat or animal products plus vegetables or hay.
Harvesting haygrass beats letting animals graze it. A haygrass plant gives 18 hay (0.90 nutrition) when harvested, but only about 0.30 if eaten where it stands.

li.heading: In the barn
li.text: Put a food stockpile inside the pen or barn, with a higher priority than your main storage, so hay gets moved there. To size the stock, read each animal's "Food consumption" on its info card; big animals eat far more than small ones.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: haygrass
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The best feed per tile for animals: harvest it, don't let them graze it
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Harvested haygrass feeds about three times what grazing it does.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Haygrass produces more per tile than any other plant, but people can't eat hay: it's for your animals. Stockpiled hay keeps grazing animals fed through winter, when there's nothing left to graze.

li.text:
Haygrass takes 7 listed grow days, about 12.9 real days, and yields 18 hay per plant. Its fertility sensitivity is 0.6, and on soil it harvests 1.39 per tile per day, the best of any plant. It can't be grown in hydroponics. Hay gives 0.05 nutrition per unit, rots in 60 days, and can also be made into straw matting.
Harvest it rather than letting animals graze it: a full-grown plant eaten in place gives about 0.30 nutrition, while its 18 hay give 0.90 once harvested. Grow haygrass through the summer, keep animals out of the field with fences or allowed areas, and store the hay in or next to the barn so the animals eat there once grazing stops.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: hunting safely
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Meat rots in 2 days, and some prey fights back
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Shooting one animal in a herd can bring the rest after the hunter.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Hunting turns wildlife into meat, but the meat rots fast and some animals fight back, sometimes as a whole herd. A badly chosen target can send a hunter home on a stretcher or start a manhunter pack, and manhunter packs carry 40% more raid points than a regular raid. Pick your prey, and have the butcher and the freezer ready before you shoot.

li.heading: Choosing hunter and prey
li.text: Hunters with short-range weapons often die against thick-skinned animals, especially early in a colony. Hunt with the longest-range gun or bow you have, and never send a melee-only hunter. Check an animal's info card before you mark it, and leave herds and big predators alone early on.

points.li: Boomalopes and boomrats burst into flame when they die. Kill them far from buildings, or in the rain.
Scaria-infected corpses rot instantly, so their meat is lost.
During toxic fallout, wildlife can be hunted for roughly the first day. Animals with heavy toxic buildup rot on death, but boomrats and boomalopes stay and can be hunted later.

li.heading: After the kill
li.text: Raw meat rots in 2 days without refrigeration, so butcher and freeze it the same day, or cook it right away. Keep the butcher table in its own room between the freezer and the kitchen.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: healroot
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Your own herbal medicine: slow, but the only home-grown kind
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Herbal medicine tends wounds twice as well as bare hands.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Healroot is the only crop that gives you medicine. Tending without medicine gives only 30% potency and herbal medicine gives 60%, so a steady patch means your doctor never has to tend wounds with bare hands.

li.heading: Growing it
li.text:
Healroot takes 7 listed grow days, about 12.9 real days, and yields 1 herbal medicine per plant: only 0.08 medicine per tile per day on soil. Sowing it needs Plants skill 8, so plant a patch as soon as someone reaches Plants 8, before a raid or a plague uses up the medicine you have.
Its fertility sensitivity is 1.0, so put it on your best soil. Unlike most crops, it's cold-resistant.

li.heading: Wild healroot
li.text: To harvest wild healroot, lay a growing zone over it with sowing switched off and cutting allowed.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: strawberries and berries
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Berries can be eaten raw without the raw-food mood penalty
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Milk, berries and insect jelly are the raw foods that carry no mood penalty.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Strawberries and wild berries are the exception to the raw-food rule: colonists can eat them straight without the -7 "ate raw food" penalty. That makes them a lifeline for a crisis start with no stove. They can still cause food poisoning, though, and cooking them into meals gets you more nutrition.

li.heading: Strawberries and wild bushes

table.li: Plant | Grow days | Yield | How you get it
Strawberries | 4.6 listed (about 8.5 real) | 8 per plant | Sown in fields or hydroponics basins
Wild berry bush | 6 | 10 per harvest | Can't be planted; harvested again and again with a cut-only growing zone

li.after: Strawberries have a fertility sensitivity of 1.0 and harvest 0.94 per tile per day on soil and 2.64 in hydroponics, so try them in basins if you want a crop besides rice. Berries rot in 14 days.

li.heading: In a crisis start
li.text: With no stove, forage wild berries first and sow strawberries early. Once you have a stove, cook them anyway: meals stretch the food further.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: wild food plants
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Agave, berry bushes and ambrosia can be harvested but never planted
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Wild plants can be harvested again and again, but you can't choose where they grow.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Some useful plants only grow wild: you can't sow them, but you can harvest them again and again when they ripen. On a harsh map, wild agave and berry bushes can carry a new colony until the first crops come in.

li.heading: What grows wild

table.li: Agave | 6 | 10 agave fruit, more than once
Wild berry bush | 6 | 10 berries, again and again

li.after: Agave fruit gives 0.05 nutrition each and rots in 25 days. Agave has a fertility sensitivity of 0.5, ambrosia 0.15.

li.heading: Harvesting them
li.text: Wild plants can't be sown, but a growing zone set to cut only harvests them when ripe. Lay one over the wild berry bushes, agave and healroot near your base. In the early days, before your fields produce, mark ripe wild plants for harvest as well, and when an ambrosia grove appears, harvest it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: cotton
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The standard cloth crop for clothes and furniture
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Cotton grows nearly three times as fast in hydroponics as on soil.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Cotton is your everyday textile: shirts, pants, beds and more. It grows at a steady pace and does well in hydroponics if you have basins to spare.

li.text: Cotton takes 8 listed grow days, about 14.8 real days, and yields 10 cloth per plant. It harvests 0.68 per tile per day on soil and 1.9 in hydroponics. Its fertility sensitivity is 1.0, so grow it on good soil, and start the patch early so clothes can be replaced before they wear out. Grazing animals will eat the plants, which are worth 0.2 nutrition to them, so keep them out of the field.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: devilstrand
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A slow, skilled crop that makes tough, heat-resistant cloth
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Devilstrand cloth makes tougher, more heat-resistant apparel than cotton.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Devilstrand is a fiber crop that takes a very long time to grow and needs a skilled grower, but its cloth makes some of the best apparel you can tailor. Expect the first harvest more than a month after sowing.

li.heading: A long season
li.text:
Devilstrand takes 22.5 listed grow days, about 41.5 real days, so sow it right at the start of the growing season. Where the season is shorter than the roughly 42 days it needs, it won't ripen outdoors at all, and it can't be grown in hydroponics.
Sowing it needs Plants 10. Each plant yields 6, only 0.14 per tile per day on soil, and with a fertility sensitivity of 1.0 it wants rich soil. With Biotech, it grows on polluted soil.

li.heading: The cloth
li.text: Devilstrand apparel resists heat well, which helps against fire. Tailor it into clothing for your fighters and firefighters.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: smokeleaf and psychoid
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The drug crops: leaves for joints, psychite tea, flake and yayo
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Yayo takes twice as many psychoid leaves as flake or tea.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Smokeleaf and psychoid are the drug crops. Their leaves feed the drug lab: smokeleaf becomes joints, and psychoid becomes psychite tea (4 leaves), flake (4 leaves) or yayo (8 leaves). Grow them only if you mean to use or sell the drugs.

li.heading: The two crops

table.li: Harvest per tile per day on soil | 0.65 | 0.48

li.after: In hydroponics, smokeleaf harvests 1.82 per tile per day. Put psychoid on poor ground and smokeleaf on good soil. With Biotech, psychoid is one of the few plants that grows on polluted ground.

li.heading: Before the stockpile fills
li.text: Set a drug policy before you stock drugs, so colonists don't help themselves. Check your ideoligion first, too: some forbid drugs outright.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: hops
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The beer crop: hops feed the brewery and its barrels
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Beer goes from field to barrel without any electricity.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Hops become beer, which is recreation that cheers people up, though too much brings hangovers. The whole chain runs without electricity, which makes it a favorite for tribal colonies.

li.heading: From field to barrel

points.li: Grow the hops: 5 listed grow days (about 9.2 real) and 8 hops per plant. They harvest 0.87 per tile per day on soil and 1.96 in hydroponics.
Brew the hops into wort at a brewery.
Ferment the wort into beer in barrels, kept in a heated or cooled room between 7 and 32 °C so batches aren't ruined.

li.after: A small hops patch goes a long way, and with a fertility sensitivity of 0.7 it copes with middling soil.

li.heading: Drinking it
li.text: Beer carries a 1% addiction chance. Set a drug policy for beer so nobody drinks themselves into a hangover before a raid.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: fishing
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A fishing zone on shallow water feeds you without a field
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Catches get bigger as a pond's fish population rises, so don't fish one down to nothing.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Fishing pulls food out of shallow water with a fishing zone, which makes it a useful extra food source for lakeside and coastal colonies. Fish in a body of water share one stock that regrows slowly, so heavy fishing thins it out.

li.heading: Setting up a zone
li.text:
Fishing needs the Fishing research; new tribal starts begin with it. A fishing zone goes on shallow, non-toxic water that holds fish, and bigger bodies of water are better, so put the zone on the largest clean, shallow water near your base. There's no fishing in the scarlands.
The Animals skill sets fishing speed and yield, so assign fishing to your best Animals colonist.

li.heading: What comes up
li.text: A catch is rolled roughly every 7,500 ticks.
li.after: With Biotech, pollution can turn up to 60% of catches into toxfish. Raw fish give 0.25 to 0.5 nutrition and rot in 2 days, as fast as meat, so freeze or cook the catch the same day.

li.heading: Keeping the stock up
li.text: All fish in one body of water share a count that regrows 2.5% of its maximum per day, unless gill rot strikes. Catch size grows from 1x to 6x as the fish population rises toward 300, so a pond fished down gives small catches. Check the fish count in the zone's inspect pane, and move to another body of water if it runs low.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: feeding children and babies
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Kids eat less, babies eat twice a day, and growth vats eat a lot
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A baby eats little at a time but must be fed twice a day.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A child's food store scales with their smaller body size, so children fill up on less food. Babies need less nutrition to become full, but their hunger is tuned so they still need feeding twice a day, by an adult or with baby food. Growth vats are a separate option that uses a lot of nutrition every day.

li.heading: Babies
li.text:
Check each baby's Feeding tab and make sure someone is free to feed them. Keep baby food stocked as well, so feeding doesn't depend on a busy adult. It's made at a campfire or stove, where 0.25 vegetable nutrition makes 10 units of 0.05 nutrition each. Baby food rots in 14 days and tastes "Terrible".
One reading of the game files puts a baby's hunger rate at about 0.125x, but the exact figure is unconfirmed.

li.heading: Growth vats
li.text: A growth vat uses 3 nutrition a day to age a child and 6 a day to grow an embryo, plus 200 W of power. Count a vat raising a child as nearly two extra adults at the table. Keep vats fed and powered, and deal with a bio-starvation warning right away.
